paragraphs: This paper develops a dataset and models for connecting touch with images and language. The challenge is both practical and representational: tactile readings need useful language labels, and their information must be aligned with what a camera observes. The dataset contains 44,000 vision–touch pairs collected in the wild, with human annotations for 10% and GPT-4V-generated textual labels for the remaining 90%.

The authors use these examples to train a tactile encoder aligned with vision and language. This encoder supports open-vocabulary classification and becomes part of a touch–vision–language model that generates text. The approach gives tactile measurements a representation that can participate in tasks involving the other two modalities.

The results suggest improved alignment, with a reported 29% classification accuracy improvement over models trained on pairs of modalities. On a new touch–vision understanding benchmark, the model also reports improvements of 12% over GPT-4V and 32% over open-source vision-language models. These findings support the usefulness of adding touch even when most language labels are generated automatically.
icml-2024-a-touch-vision-and-language-da.tldr: A dataset of 44,000 vision–touch pairs supports models that connect tactile sensing with images and language, improving reported multimodal understanding.

paragraphs: Generating language one token at a time creates a hardware bottleneck: decoding can be limited by memory bandwidth while leaving much of an accelerator’s parallel computing capacity unused. Lookahead decoding addresses this mismatch with an exact parallel decoding algorithm. Its aim is to reduce the number of sequential decoding steps needed to produce output.

The method trades additional computation within a step for fewer steps overall. This changes how available hardware is used, making decoding more parallelizable on either one accelerator or several. It requires neither an auxiliary draft model nor a data store, and it can operate alongside memory-efficient attention implementations such as FlashAttention.

The implementation reports speedups of up to 1.8 times on MT-bench and up to four times for code completion when scaling across multiple GPUs. These are reported outcomes for those settings, with the larger result explicitly involving multiple devices. The contribution is an exact decoding route that uses extra parallel computation to reduce latency without requiring a separately obtained draft model.
icml-2024-break-the-sequential-dependenc.tldr: Lookahead decoding uses parallel computation to accelerate exact LLM decoding without an auxiliary model or data store.

paragraphs: Transformers can learn to solve tasks from examples supplied in their context, but training this ability can involve long periods of little improvement. This paper investigates these learning plateaus by separating the model’s internal representation conceptually into two parts. One part depends exclusively on the model’s weights; the remaining part is called the context component.

Controlled experiments on synthetic tasks connect persistent plateaus with impaired functioning of the weights component. This decomposition gives the authors a way to examine which part of the representation is associated with stalled progress. The reported correlation motivates their account of why learning can remain slow even while training continues.

Building on that diagnosis, the authors develop three strategies to accelerate Transformer learning and confirm their effectiveness on natural language processing tasks. The abstract does not enumerate those strategies, but it establishes the connection between the internal analysis and the interventions. The findings support the feasibility of training strong in-context learning abilities more efficiently by addressing the behavior associated with plateaus.
icml-2024-breaking-through-the-learning-.tldr: An analysis of Transformer representations links in-context learning plateaus to an impaired weights component and motivates three training acceleration strategies.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks commonly update each node by collecting messages from its neighbors. Repeating this process lets node representations incorporate information from the surrounding graph. This paper introduces a training framework that gives each node more control over that communication, treating nodes as players that choose how to participate.

A node can listen, broadcast, do both, or isolate itself. Its choice depends on its current state, allowing the communication pattern to change as learning progresses. Standard message passing fits inside this framework as the particular case in which every node both listens and broadcasts to all its neighbors.

This flexibility makes communication itself part of the learning process. Different node states can lead to different patterns of information exchange, effectively exploring the graph’s topology while building representations. The paper provides theoretical analysis of the proposed scheme and supports it with experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets. The stated contribution is a broader, dynamic message-passing framework whose behavior is examined through both mathematical and empirical analysis.
icml-2024-cooperative-graph-neural-netwo.tldr: Cooperative graph neural networks let each node choose whether to send, receive, or avoid messages based on its current state.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theory of how finite network width affects feature learning in deep nonlinear networks. It describes the network’s Bayesian prior as a mixture of Gaussian processes, with variation among their kernels decreasing inversely with network width. These kernels describe the relationships between inputs that the network represents.

The authors use a large-deviation analysis to obtain coupled forward and backward equations for the most probable kernels across all layers. The analysis is exact in a proportional limit where dataset size and network width grow together at a fixed ratio. A perturbative study of the equations shows how backward propagation aligns kernels with the prediction target.

A complementary field-theoretic formulation connects adaptation after observing data to fluctuations already present in the prior. Larger fluctuations make the prior more flexible and permit stronger adaptation. This connects finite-width feature learning with edge-of-chaos Gaussian-process theory, showing how criticality, response behavior, and feature scale interact within the analyzed framework.
icml-2024-critical-feature-learning-in-d.tldr: A finite-width kernel theory links feature learning to fluctuations in a network’s Bayesian prior and their alignment with training targets.

paragraphs: This paper studies how continued pretraining can extend language models to contexts of 128,000 tokens. Its starting hypothesis is that large-scale pretraining already develops much of the ability to use information at arbitrary input positions. An appropriate additional training mixture may then extend that capability far beyond the context lengths previously encountered.

The study examines both data quantity and data composition. It reports that 500 million to five billion tokens can enable retrieval of information throughout a 128,000-token context. The composition results emphasize two requirements together: increasing the representation of long examples and maintaining balance across domains. Simply emphasizing long material from domains such as books produces suboptimal results.

The authors present full-model continued pretraining on one to five billion suitably mixed tokens as an effective, affordable recipe. Their models outperform strong open-source long-context models and narrow the gap to GPT-4 128K. These findings make data engineering central to the proposed extension strategy, while the idea that the underlying capability is largely acquired earlier remains the paper’s motivating hypothesis.
icml-2024-data-engineering-for-scaling-l.tldr: Balanced domains and increased exposure to long examples make continued pretraining an effective route to 128,000-token language-model contexts.

paragraphs: Many explanation methods use cooperative game theory to assign credit for a model’s prediction. This paper identifies a mismatch that can arise when the desired explanation concerns the model’s output, but the method attributes only a scalar quantity such as one class’s probability. A change in that number does not by itself describe all the relevant behavior of the output.

The authors generalize cooperative games and their value operators to introduce distributional values. These are random variables that track changes in model output, including events such as a predicted class switching. The framework therefore represents attribution in a form that can express probabilistic output changes more directly.

The paper derives analytic expressions for Gaussian, Bernoulli, and categorical payoffs and establishes properties that characterize the resulting values. Case studies involving vision and language models demonstrate fine-grained explanations. The contribution is a mathematical framework for bringing the object being explained closer to the behavior a user wants to understand, with demonstrations of how that richer description can be informative.
icml-2024-explaining-probabilistic-model.tldr: Distributional values extend game-theoretic explanations to describe probabilistic changes in model outputs, including changes of predicted class.

paragraphs: This paper studies fairness when learning a decision policy from observational records. The data are explicitly assumed to come from a different behavioral policy, which may itself be discriminatory. That setting matters because learning a new decision rule involves evidence shaped by earlier decisions, rather than observations collected under the policy now being developed.

The proposed neural network framework learns optimal policies under different definitions of fairness. Those definitions can concern the actions a policy takes or the values associated with the policy. This distinction lets the framework address fairness at different points in decision-making, rather than treating fairness solely as a property of predictions.

The authors provide generalization bounds for the finite-sample framework and evaluate it using simulated and real-world data. The experiments demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness in the studied settings, while the theoretical results address how learning from a finite dataset relates to broader performance. Together, these contributions connect explicit fairness requirements with policy learning from records produced by a potentially discriminatory predecessor.
icml-2024-fair-off-policy-learning-from-.tldr: A neural framework learns policies under action-based or value-based fairness requirements from data collected by a potentially discriminatory policy.

paragraphs: The paper considers agents that repeatedly choose subsets of available arms and observe a noisy reward for the entire subset. They cannot see each arm’s individual contribution, but they can periodically share information. This combines combinatorial decision-making, limited feedback, and cooperation without requiring constant communication.

The framework converts an offline single-agent approximation algorithm into an online multi-agent algorithm, provided the original algorithm satisfies the stated resilience and complexity requirements. Its guarantee measures regret against an approximation benchmark. The resulting bound grows sublinearly with time and improves with the number of communicating agents, while removing the original epsilon approximation error. Communication rounds also grow sublinearly.

The authors apply the conversion to stochastic submodular maximization using several offline algorithms. They obtain new results for single-agent and multi-agent settings and recover specialized single-agent guarantees. Experiments on stochastic data summarization demonstrate effectiveness even with one agent. The central contribution is a reusable connection between qualifying offline optimization procedures and cooperative online learning with provable performance and communication bounds.
icml-2024-federated-combinatorial-multi-.tldr: A federated framework converts qualifying offline approximation algorithms into cooperative online bandit algorithms with sublinear regret and communication.

paragraphs: FuRL investigates how pretrained visual-language models can help agents learn online when task rewards are sparse. The setting includes a predefined textual description of the task. Such descriptions make visual-language models a potential source of reward guidance, but the paper identifies a problem: their rewards can be misaligned with the reinforcement learning objective.

The proposed method combines reward alignment with relay reinforcement learning. It uses lightweight fine-tuning of visual-language representations to improve their usefulness as a reward signal. Relay reinforcement learning provides the other part of the method, helping the agent avoid local minima during learning. The two components address the quality of the guidance and the learning behavior that uses it.

Experiments on Meta-world tasks show improvements to SAC and DrQ agents in the sparse-reward setting. The findings support adapting pretrained visual-language representations when using them to guide online reinforcement learning. In the reported experiments, the combined method makes that guidance more effective for agents learning from otherwise infrequent task rewards.
icml-2024-furl-visual-language-models-as.tldr: FuRL combines lightweight visual-language reward alignment with relay reinforcement learning to improve agents on sparse-reward tasks.

paragraphs: HALO addresses which pixels should be labeled when adapting a semantic segmentation model to a different domain. The approach uses a hyperbolic neural network and interprets the radius of its representations as an indicator of data scarcity. This links the geometry of the learned representation to where additional labeled information may be useful.

The acquisition strategy targets epistemic uncertainty: uncertainty associated with what the model has insufficient knowledge about. HALO approximates this using hyperbolic radius together with prediction entropy. Combining the two signals guides label acquisition toward data points that the model knows least, giving the geometry a direct role in choosing annotation targets.

The authors evaluate synthetic-to-real transfer from GTAV and SYNTHIA to Cityscapes, along with Cityscapes-to-ACDC adaptation under adverse weather. They test convolutional and attention-based backbones. The paper reports state-of-the-art active-learning performance under domain shift and surpassing supervised domain adaptation using only 1% of labels. These results support the proposed uncertainty approximation as an effective way to spend a small annotation budget in the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-hyperbolic-active-learning-for.tldr: HALO combines hyperbolic geometry and prediction entropy to select informative pixels for labeling during segmentation domain adaptation.

paragraphs: HypDiff is a graph-generation framework that performs diffusion in a geometrically structured latent space. The paper motivates this choice through two challenges: discrete graph diffusion can be computationally expensive, while existing latent approaches can struggle to retain graph topology. The organization of a graph is not equally represented in every latent direction.

The authors construct a hyperbolic latent space with interpretable geometric measures and define an anisotropic diffusion process within it. Anisotropy means that the process accounts for differences between directions. Both radial and angular properties constrain the diffusion, connecting how latent representations change to the structural information the generated graphs should preserve.

The proposed geometry therefore shapes the generation process itself, with the stated aim of preserving original topological properties. Extensive experiments report superior effectiveness across graphs with various topologies. The contribution is a latent diffusion framework that explicitly incorporates geometric structure into graph generation, alongside empirical evidence that this design handles a variety of graph organizations effectively.
icml-2024-hyperbolic-geometric-latent-di.tldr: HypDiff uses radially and angularly constrained diffusion in a hyperbolic latent space to preserve topology during graph generation.

paragraphs: This paper shows theoretically that a classifier can favor a single class before training begins. A deep network’s structure can cause all its predictions to fall into the same class even without explicit biases. The authors call this phenomenon Initial Guessing Bias, emphasizing that a systematic preference can already exist at initialization.

The analysis identifies several factors that influence whether this behavior occurs. Dataset properties matter, but so do preprocessing choices, activation functions, max-pooling layers, and network depth. These findings connect the initial prediction pattern to concrete modeling decisions and provide information relevant to selecting architectures and initialization procedures.

The theory also identifies consequences involving node-permutation symmetry, self-averaging, and the effects of depth. In particular, the reported violation of self-averaging highlights that averaging behavior need not describe an individual network’s behavior in the expected way. Overall, the paper establishes that untrained classification behavior deserves analysis in its own right, because architecture and preprocessing can shape class preferences before any learning from labels occurs.
icml-2024-initial-guessing-bias-how-untr.tldr: Network architecture and preprocessing can make an untrained classifier assign every input to one class, even without explicit biases.

paragraphs: Researchers often simplify neural representations to make them easier to inspect, for example by projecting hidden states into fewer dimensions. This paper examines whether those simplified representations remain faithful when a model encounters unfamiliar inputs. Its central concern is that accurately approximating training behavior may not establish how well a proxy describes generalization.

The authors train Transformers on controlled datasets with systematic generalization splits, including balanced-parenthesis languages and code completion. They then create simplified proxies using dimensionality reduction and clustering. By explicitly comparing proxy behavior with the original models, they test fidelity both within the familiar distribution and on systematic generalization tasks.

The experiments find consistent gaps between these settings. Sometimes the original model generalizes systematically while its simplified proxy fails; sometimes the proxy generalizes better than the original. Either direction creates a mismatch for interpretation. The findings therefore question whether mechanistic conclusions drawn from tools such as singular value decomposition can reliably predict behavior in novel situations merely because the simplification matches familiar examples.
icml-2024-interpretability-illusions-in-.tldr: Simplified Transformer representations can match familiar behavior yet misrepresent generalization, with proxies sometimes performing worse or better than the original model.

paragraphs: This paper studies estimation of conditional average treatment effects: how an intervention’s average effect varies with observed characteristics. Many estimators can be written as regressions on transformed outcomes, called pseudo-outcomes, with observations receiving different weights. The authors argue that these weights can be the dominant source of performance differences, despite previous comparisons emphasizing the outcome transformation.

Their focus is inverse-variance weighting, which adjusts observations’ influence according to their variability. They show that R-Learning already has an implicit interpretation as pseudo-outcome regression with these weights. In this treatment-effect setting, inverse-variance weights reduce instability associated with inverse-propensity weighting and simplify terms appearing in the bias analysis.

Simulations demonstrate superior performance for inverse-variance weighting, and the paper derives convergence rates. The authors qualify these as the fastest they know of without assuming the covariate distribution is known. The results give both an empirical and theoretical reason to examine weighting choices carefully when comparing or constructing treatment-effect estimators, rather than attributing their behavior mainly to pseudo-outcome design.
icml-2024-inverse-variance-weighting-for.tldr: Inverse-variance weighting improves treatment-effect estimation in simulations and yields strong convergence rates without assuming a known covariate distribution.

paragraphs: This paper develops an algorithm for discovering reusable skills from expert demonstrations. The starting material is a collection of trajectories, which must be divided into meaningful pieces before those pieces can become useful skills. A large language model proposes the initial segmentation, supplying information that guides the subsequent learning process.

A hierarchical variational inference framework incorporates those proposed boundaries and discovers skills by merging trajectory segments. An additional objective based on the Minimum Description Length principle controls the trade-off between compression and reusability. This gives the method an explicit way to balance a compact description of demonstrations against the usefulness of the resulting skills across tasks.

The authors evaluate agents on new long-horizon tasks in BabyAI, a grid navigation environment, and ALFRED, a household simulation environment. The discovered skills accelerate learning and outperform the compared skill-learning baselines. These results support a staged approach in which language-model segmentation informs statistical skill discovery, with the compression objective helping shape skills that transfer to later tasks.
icml-2024-language-guided-skill-learning.tldr: Language-model trajectory segmentation guides a variational skill-discovery method that improves learning on new long-horizon tasks.

paragraphs: This paper proposes an optimization algorithm for a special class of nonlinear objectives whose inputs are probability measures. In these problems, the quantity being optimized is a distribution. The abstract identifies training mean-field neural networks, minimizing maximum mean discrepancy, and minimizing kernel Stein discrepancy as examples that fit this formulation.

The proposed N-particle underdamped Langevin algorithm comes from a new discretization of mean-field underdamped Langevin dynamics in both space and time. This connects a continuous mathematical process to a finite-particle procedure that can be implemented. The authors also establish a new fast-mixing guarantee for the underlying dynamics, addressing how quickly the process approaches its limiting behavior.

A further result proves global convergence of the algorithm in total variation distance, a measure of discrepancy between probability distributions. This is important because a guarantee for continuous dynamics alone does not complete the analysis of a discretized implementation. The paper’s contribution covers both levels, linking the mathematical dynamics and the practical algorithm for the stated class of objectives.
icml-2024-mean-field-underdamped-langevi.tldr: A new particle-based Langevin algorithm connects fast-mixing mean-field dynamics to a discretized implementation with global total-variation convergence.

paragraphs: This paper combines explicit mathematical modeling and neural learning to reconstruct missing values in optical flow fields. Its architecture joins a partial differential equation approach with convolutional neural networks. The motivation is to bring specialized domain knowledge into a learned system while retaining the ability to adapt from data.

The explicit component supplies a mathematically specified model, while the neural component contributes data-driven modeling. The authors evaluate the resulting joint architecture against fully explicit and fully data-driven approaches. They report advantages in reconstruction quality, robustness, and the amount of training data required, supporting the usefulness of combining the two approaches for this task.

When endpoint error is averaged over different mask densities, the method improves on explicit baselines by 11–27%, the GAN baseline by 47%, and the probabilistic diffusion baseline by 42%. The paper reports a new state of the art for optical-flow inpainting from random masks. That random-mask setting defines the stated reconstruction result and anchors the numerical comparisons to the evaluated task.
icml-2024-neuroexplicit-diffusion-models.tldr: Combining PDE-based modeling with convolutional networks improves optical-flow inpainting quality, robustness, and training-data requirements in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: PinNet addresses a failure mode in generating descriptions of code with retrieved references. Retrieval can provide useful material, but a reference may also contain irrelevant or misleading information. A generator that gives this material too much influence can produce a worse description despite having access to additional examples.

The framework uses a discriminator to assess how well retrieved material matches the meaning of the input code. It then uses the discriminator’s hidden representation, taken before its output layer, to modify the generator’s attention weights. This makes semantic matching influence which parts of a reference receive attention during generation.

The authors also introduce a contrastive learning method for measuring semantic similarity among unlabeled references. Experiments on code summarization and SQL-to-text generation show significant improvements over all compared baselines. The findings support using the internal representation of a relevance-assessing model to guide generation, helping useful reference information receive more attention while reducing the influence of misleading content.
icml-2024-pinnet-pinpoint-instructive-in.tldr: PinNet uses a discriminator’s semantic representations to guide attention toward useful retrieved information when generating descriptions of code.

paragraphs: Value-based reinforcement learning often requires finding the highest-valued action among every available choice. With a large discrete action space, that repeated search can become expensive, particularly when a neural network approximates the value function. This paper reduces the search burden by considering a changing random subset of actions at each iteration.

The proposed subset sizes grow sublinearly with the total number of actions and can be as small as logarithmic in that number. The approach is applied to both value updates and action selection. The resulting methods include Stochastic Q-learning, StochDQN, and StochDDQN, extending the same computational idea across several value-based learning algorithms.

The paper establishes theoretical convergence for Stochastic Q-learning and analyzes stochastic maximization. Empirical evaluations across diverse environments, including control tasks, show the proposed approaches outperforming the compared baselines and achieving near-optimal average returns in substantially less time. The theoretical convergence claim specifically concerns Stochastic Q-learning, while the broader family receives experimental support for reducing computation without losing strong returns in the studied tasks.
icml-2024-stochastic-q-learning-for-larg.tldr: Stochastic value-based reinforcement learning searches small random action subsets, reducing computation while achieving strong empirical returns.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes generative models trained in a recursive loop, where each generation learns from real data mixed with synthetic data produced by earlier models. The central question is how the generated distribution changes across generations relative to the original real-data distribution. The framework considers both parametric and nonparametric models.

For diffusion models with a one-hidden-layer neural network score function, the authors bound this discrepancy using total variation distance under several mixed-training scenarios. They show that the distance can be controlled when the mixed datasets are sufficiently large or the proportion of real data is sufficiently high. These are sufficient conditions within the analyzed settings.

The theory also identifies a phase transition as synthetic-data quantities increase: the distance initially grows, then decreases beyond a threshold. This makes the relationship between synthetic-data volume and distributional error nonmonotonic in the analysis. Additional results for kernel density estimation examine how mixed-data training affects error propagation, extending the investigation beyond the specified diffusion-model formulation.
icml-2024-towards-theoretical-understand.tldr: Theoretical bounds show conditions under which recursively mixing real and synthetic training data can control generative distribution drift.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning can train an agent using trajectories generated by a learned transition model. These simulated rollouts are useful only to the extent that the model’s predictions are sufficiently accurate. This paper focuses on the fact that accuracy varies locally, making a single rollout-length schedule an incomplete guide to where generated experience is trustworthy.

MACURA uses the model’s own uncertainty to account for those local differences. Its uncertainty-aware rollout adaptation mechanism bases trust on the region being modeled, rather than relying solely on the stage of training. The authors describe the rollout mechanism as easy to tune and integrate it into a model-based actor-critic algorithm.

Experiments on the MuJoCo benchmark report substantial improvements in data efficiency and performance over state-of-the-art deep model-based reinforcement learning methods. These findings support using local uncertainty to guide model-generated experience in the evaluated tasks. The paper’s contribution is to make the decision about useful rollouts sensitive to where the predictive model is operating, including the concern that accuracy can deteriorate when extrapolating.
icml-2024-trust-the-model-where-it-trust.tldr: MACURA adapts model-generated rollouts using local model uncertainty, improving data efficiency and performance on MuJoCo.

paragraphs: A counterfactual explanation changes an input so that a classifier produces a different decision. This paper highlights that the changed decision may leave the true underlying class probabilities unaffected. In that case, the modification can resemble an adversarial attack: it changes the classifier’s response without delivering the underlying improvement that the user seeks.

The authors introduce Trustworthy Actionable Perturbations, a framework aimed at beneficial changes in true class probabilities. A new verification procedure is designed to distinguish such changes from adversarial behavior. The framework also revises the definitions of cost, reward, and goals to better reflect the objective of producing meaningful changes in the real world.

The paper provides PAC-learnability results for the verification procedure and a theoretical analysis of its reward measure. It also develops a method for creating these perturbations and compares it with earlier counterfactual approaches. The contribution connects generating a proposed modification with verifying the kind of probabilistic improvement it is meant to achieve, making the underlying target of a changed decision explicit.
icml-2024-trustworthy-actionable-perturb.tldr: Trustworthy Actionable Perturbations pair input modifications with verification aimed at improving true class probabilities rather than merely changing classifier outputs.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to pretrain a generalist agent from unlabeled offline trajectories and then use it for new tasks without further task-specific training. Its proposed functional reward encoding represents a task through samples pairing states with rewards. A transformer-based variational autoencoder learns to turn these samples into a functional representation.

The same representation supports pretraining across diverse unsupervised reward functions and specifying a downstream task using a small number of reward-annotated samples. This provides a common interface between the tasks used during pretraining and those encountered later. Zero-shot adaptation here still receives reward information describing the new task through those samples.

Experiments on simulated robotic benchmarks show that agents pretrained with diverse random reward functions can solve novel tasks. They often outperform earlier zero-shot reinforcement learning and offline reinforcement learning methods. The findings support functional reward encoding as a scalable approach to task representation, with empirical evidence that diversity in unsupervised pretraining rewards can support later generalization to new objectives.
icml-2024-unsupervised-zero-shot-reinfor.tldr: Functional reward encodings let pretrained agents tackle new tasks from a few reward-annotated samples, with strong results on simulated robotics benchmarks.

paragraphs: Graph-learning architectures are often compared by their ability to distinguish graphs with different structures. The Weisfeiler–Leman procedure, especially 1-WL, is a standard reference for this kind of expressivity. This paper asks how much such distinctions actually reveal about generalization, finding that expressivity viewed through graph isomorphism gives only limited insight into predictive performance.

The authors examine versions of 1-WL and message-passing graph neural networks augmented with subgraph information. They use classical margin theory to study conditions under which greater expressivity is associated with improved generalization. This shifts attention toward how the resulting representations support separation in a learning problem, alongside which graphs they can distinguish.

The paper also introduces expressive 1-WL-based kernel and neural architectures with provable generalization properties. An empirical study supports the theoretical findings. The overall result is a more conditional account of why additional graph information can help: increased expressive power becomes informative when connected to the generalization conditions studied, rather than serving as a sufficient performance ranking by itself.
icml-2024-weisfeiler-leman-at-the-margin.tldr: Margin-based analysis identifies conditions linking richer graph representations to better generalization, beyond expressivity measured by graph distinction alone.
